Beállítom A jövő hétre rendkívüli parlamenti ülés összehívását kezdeményezte Ruff Bálint Miniszterelnökséget vezető miniszter. Az indítványban szerepel, hogy mi kerülne az augusztus 10–11 napokon tartott ülés napirendjére. Ez alapján a közneveléssel, a rendvédelmi szervekkel és a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatallal kapcsolatos törvényeket is módosítanák. Ezen a héten a hőség okozta válsághelyzet miatt nem ült össze az országgyűlés . Az indítvány indoklása szerint a mostani energiakrízis fényében az akkumulátorüzemekre vonatkozó szabályokat is módosítanák, hogy átláthatóbb és környezetvédelmileg biztonságosabb szabályozást alkossanak. Emellett szerepel a javaslatok között az is, hogy a vényköteles gyógyszerek áfáját 5 százalékról 0 százalékra csökkentsék, ezt már korábban megígérte a kormány . Ruff Bálint javaslata szerint a következőket tárgyalnák a jövő hét rendkívüli ülésén: Egyes egészségügyi adatkezelést érintő törvények módosítását. A közneveléssel kapcsolatos egyes törvények módosítását. Egyes törvények a rendészeti feladatellátás racionalizálását. A Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatallal összefüggő költségvetési címrendmódosítását. A vészhelyzet megszüntetésével összefüggő átmeneti szabályokról és a járványügyi készültségről szóló 2020 évi LVIII. törvény módosítását. A Magyar Agrár-, Élelmiszergazdasági és Vidékfejlesztési Kamaráról szóló 2012. évi CXXVI. törvény módosítását. A közpénzügyi reformokkal összefüggésben egyes államháztartási szabályok módosítását. A Magyarország 2026. évi központi költségvetéséről szóló 2025. évi LXIX. törvény módosítását. A szakképzésről szóló 2019. évi LXXX. törvény módosítását. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text: Disabled bus pass holders in England will be able to travel for free at all hours from April next year, the government has announced. Currently, disabled bus passes are valid for travel only on weekdays from 9.30am to 11pm unless local authorities fund an extension, as Greater Manchester did earlier this year when Andy Burnham was mayor. The prime minister, who is announcing the changes as part of his drive to reduce the cost of living, said it was “simply not right that many disabled people cannot travel using their pass during certain times of the day”. The £60m to fund the move comes from existing budgets – with £40m from the Department for Work and Pensions and £20m from the Department for Transport. Burnham is visiting a bus station in the West Midlands this morning and is expected to give more details on the policy then. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters European Union EU’s ability to defend against invasion remains in doubt, finds official report Fragmented infrastructure and reliance on US continue to hinder ‘defence readiness’, says European court of auditors Europe live – latest updates Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.09 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The EU’s ability to respond to a foreign invasion by 2030 remains in doubt due to a continuing reliance on the US and fragmented national defence systems, according to a report from its official auditor. The European court of auditors (ECA) said the EU was much better prepared than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine of 2022, but achieving its goal of defence readiness by the end of the decade would be difficult. “Achieving defence preparedness in the EU by 2030 remains challenging,” said Marek Opioła, an ECA member who led the review of the EU’s defence policy published on Thursday. “There are still major difficulties such as fragmented national systems or industrial bottlenecks. We also still rely on the United States.” Speaking to the Guardian, he stressed the EU could “still make major progress” if it sharply increased defence spending and rapidly expanded ammunition production. Between 2020 and 2025, EU member states increased defence spending by 79%, a response to the Russian threat and a belated effort to meet Nato spending targets. In November 2024, the EU met its pledge of providing 1 million rounds of ammunition to Ukraine – eight months behind schedule. The EU set the goal of defence readiness by 2030 last year , after intelligence services warned that Russia could be ready to wage a large-scale war in Europe around that time. The bloc’s financial watchdog said major difficulties had to be overcome to reach this target, defined by a senior auditor as “having strategic autonomy” and “the ability to independently sustain high-intensity warfare”. The senior auditor said the EU was better prepared than 2019 when a similar review was conducted, but warned that fragmented national defence industries and “insufficient cooperation” between EU governments contributed to a risk of duplication in spending or persistent gaps in military capabilities. Emblematic of the dysfunction – although not mentioned in the report – is France and Germany’s decision to abandon a €100bn project to build a joint fighter jet, because the lead companies were unable to resolve disputes over leadership and control. The report highlighted a possible tension between short-term battlefield needs and a “Buy European” policy that aims to reduce dependencies on foreign suppliers. Between February 2022 and June 2023, 78% of EU governments’ defence acquisitions were sourced outside the bloc, with the US alone representing 63%, according to one study cited by the ECA. The senior auditor said purchases from the US went up after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine “which was understandable because the EU needed to find capabilities that were available quickly”. The official added that “early signs of improvement in that situation” were visible, although the auditors did not have complete data to draw conclusions. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The EU has set requirements that common defence spending should benefit domestic defence industries or those of closely-associated countries, such as Ukraine and Norway. But some flexibilities have been allowed where Europe is unable to produce critical supplies in time. After a brutal summer of deadly Russian missile and drone attacks, this week Ukraine asked for an exemption from Buy European procurement rules to acquire US-made Patriot interceptors using the EU’s €90bn support loan. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said on Wednesday that Ukraine had requested funding “worth several billion euros” for air defences, including Patriot air-defence systems. A commission spokesperson said Ukraine’s request for Patriot interceptor missiles “would require a derogation” from rules requiring majority European content in military purchases under the loan. “The final say is with the member states and of course our hope would be that this would soon be granted,” the spokesperson said. The senior auditor said sometimes “it may make sense” to buy outside “when you have a short-term urgent need”. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Sanctions must continue, EU’s top diplomat stresses, as Russian attacks kill five Kaja Kallas says sanctions vital as bloc scrambles to reach deal on extension; UN sounds warning for civilians on both sides of war as winter approaches. What we know on day 1,672 Guardian staff and agencies Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.40 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The EU’s top diplomat has urged member countries to maintain sanctions targeting Russia, as Moscow’s forces continued their attacks on Ukraine , killing at least five people. “Sanctions are a core pillar of our response to Russia’s war”, Kaja Kallas told reporters in New York after a meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers. Officials aimed to close talks on a rollover of Russia sanctions soon and have the extension take place swiftly, she said. “We need to have this stability,” with sanctions remaining in place for a longer time, Kallas added on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. She stressed the EU’s position has not changed: “That’s why we are also working on a new package of sanctions.” Discussions on the sanctions are ongoing as some EU member states sought to remove certain individuals from the bloc’s blacklist . EU countries failed on Monday to finalise a deal that involved lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiga denounced the move to remove them as “unacceptable” and said it would send Moscow the “wrong signal”. Negotiations are set to continue in Brussels in efforts to extend sanctions on almost 3,000 other individuals and entities over the war as the bloc scrambles to reach a deal ahead of late Tuesday’s deadline. Russian forces continued their attacks on different ⁠Ukrainian regions along the 1,200km frontline on ⁠Monday, killing ​at least five people, regional officials said. Prosecutors in ⁠north-eastern Kharkiv region said a drone strike on the town of ⁠Lozova killed one person and ​injured three. Farther south ‌in Dnipropetrovsk region, ‌a drone killed a car driver ‌in Nikopol. In the Donetsk ‌region, a Russian ​strike badly damaged an apartment building in the strategic Kramatorsk, killing one person, while another person was killed in ⁠a nearby village. A sustained attack ​on ​a village in ​Mykolaiv region killed a ​three-year-old ​child. The attacks could not be independently verified. Russian also bombarded Zaporizhzhia overnight to Monday, hitting apartment blocks, a university and a shopping mall, among other sites, and wounding five people, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Donald Trump is expected to press the Ukrainian president on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Andrew Roth reports . It comes as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, and the US president said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage he said was being exacerbated by the Ukraine war. Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine , officials said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections. Luke Harding reports that the pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures, further consolidating Vladimir Putin’s grip on power. Escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches , UN investigators have warned, expressing fear of a repeat of last winter’s suffering. In a fresh update, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine warned the attacks raised concerns that already difficult living conditions could worsen dramatically with the arrival of winter, as was the case last year. Last winter, Russian forces “continued to launch systematic waves of attacks against Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure as temperatures plunged to minus 20C”, it said in a statement. “Millions of civilians endured prolonged power outages, shortages or lengthy absence of heating.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Europe explainers Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
